subtopics: Step Into, Step Over, and Step Out

content.intro: Debugging C# Applications is lesson 111 in Exceptions, Debugging, and Diagnostics. Exceptions represent failures that should interrupt the ordinary path; diagnostics should add actionable context without exposing secrets or hiding the root cause.
content.why_it_matters: Reliable programs expect failure paths and provide information that helps someone diagnose them. This lesson focuses on debugging c# applications and shows how to verify the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Exceptions represent failures that should interrupt the ordinary path; diagnostics should add actionable context without exposing secrets or hiding the root cause.

content_blocks.title: A practical way to learn it
content_blocks.text: Start with the smallest valid case for debugging c# applications. Predict the output, run or inspect the example in the stated toolchain, then change one input or rule and compare the result. For production code, record assumptions and verify boundary cases.

items.title: Breakpoints
items.text: Create a reproducible case, inspect the state at the failure boundary, and log structured context that helps diagnosis.

items.title: Step Into, Step Over, and Step Out
items.text: Pick a parameter-passing form that communicates ownership and intent; avoid ref/out when a returned value is clearer.

items.title: Inspecting variables
items.text: A variable has a type, a current value, and a scope. Initialize it before use, limit its lifetime where possible, and make state changes visible so later code can reason about it.

items.title: Watch windows
items.text: For watch windows, define the expected behavior, inspect how it relates to debugging c# applications, and verify a representative case plus one boundary or failure case.

items.title: Call stacks
items.text: Select a collection from the operations the caller needs: order, key lookup, uniqueness, FIFO/LIFO, sorted access, concurrency, or immutability. Program against the narrowest useful interface and check equality/hash-code behavior for keys.

items.title: Conditional breakpoints

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small C# example that demonstrates debugging c# applications. Change one input or implementation detail, predict the result, then check it locally and explain one edge case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates debugging c# applications rather than only repeating its definition.
The result is checked locally or against a clearly documented reference output.
At least one relevant boundary, invalid-input case, or compatibility condition is considered.
hints: List the assumptions and expected behavior for debugging c# applications before editing the code.
Change one variable or rule at a time; keep the previous output for comparison.
If behavior differs, confirm the compiler/target framework and consult the linked official documentation.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: identify the expected input and output, start from the smallest example, use the feature only where it clarifies the rule, and verify both a typical case and a boundary/failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the feature works identically on every target
common_mistakes.why: Language syntax, libraries, and runtime support are version-dependent.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the target framework and official versioned reference before using the feature.

common_mistakes.why: Boundary values, malformed input, and failure states often expose the real bug.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one typical input and one boundary or invalid case to the manual or automated checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating sample output as proof that the code ran
common_mistakes.why: The course reader uses static reference output for C# because it has no C# execution runner.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the snippet in a local .NET project or a separately isolated execution service.
